title: Review a frontend authentication implementation storing sensitive tokens unsafely
description: Problem: Review a frontend authentication implementation storing sensitive tokens unsafely. Solve this problem with multiple approaches and detailed explanations.

data.text: **Review a frontend authentication implementation storing sensitive tokens unsafely** is a critical security review. Access tokens, refresh tokens, and session secrets must be stored in a way that balances usability with protection against XSS, CSRF, and token theft. A senior review should identify where tokens live, how they are transmitted, and what happens when a user closes the tab.

items: localStorage: accessible to any script on the page, including injected XSS payloads
sessionStorage: slightly better because it is cleared on tab close, but still vulnerable to XSS
window.name: persists across navigation and is trivially readable by any script
URL query parameters: logged by servers, proxies, and browser history
Non-HttpOnly cookies without Secure and SameSite flags: vulnerable to CSRF and network interception
Redux or global state: adds unnecessary exposure and leaks tokens through DevTools

terms.definition: Cross-site scripting. An attacker injects script into a trusted page, allowing them to read tokens, cookies, or other sensitive data.
Cross-site request forgery. An attacker tricks a user's browser into sending an authenticated request to your server.
A cookie with the HttpOnly flag, which prevents JavaScript from reading it via document.cookie. It is the primary defense against token theft via XSS.
A cookie attribute that controls when the browser sends cookies with cross-site requests. Strict and Lax modes mitigate CSRF.
Issuing a new refresh token on every use and invalidating the old one. Limits the blast radius of a stolen refresh token.

cards.title: HttpOnly cookie
cards.description: Cookie inaccessible to JavaScript, sent automatically with requests.
cons: Requires CSRF token for write operations

cards.title: In-memory only
cards.description: Token stored in a React ref or variable, lost on refresh.
cons: User is logged out on refresh

cards.title: IndexedDB with encryption
cards.description: Encrypted storage accessible only through a dedicated bridge.
cons: Still accessible if encryption key is in JS

data.title: localStorage is not a secret vault
data.text: Any JavaScript running on your page can read localStorage. If your site has an XSS vulnerability, the attacker does not need to hack the network—they just call localStorage.getItem('token'). Use HttpOnly cookies for access tokens whenever possible.

The most secure frontend pattern stores the access token in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie. The refresh token is also HttpOnly. The backend handles token refresh transparently on 401 responses. CSRF is mitigated by SameSite=Lax and a double-submit CSRF cookie for sensitive write operations.

data.caption: Recommended authentication flow with HttpOnly cookies
data.definition:
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Server
    U->>C: Enter credentials
    C->>S: POST /login (body: email, password)
    S->>S: Validate credentials
    S->>C: Set-Cookie: accessToken (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax)
    S->>C: Set-Cookie: refreshToken (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax)
    C->>S: GET /api/data (cookie sent automatically)
    S->>S: Validate accessToken
    S->>C: 200 OK + data
    C->>U: Render data
    Note over C,S: On 401: POST /refresh with refreshToken cookie
    S->>C: 200 OK + new accessToken cookie
    S->>C: 401 Unauthorized (refresh also expired)
    C->>U: Redirect to /login

items: Storing the access token in Redux and logging it to the console for debugging
Passing the token in URL query parameters for deep links
Using the same token for API calls and third-party analytics
Skipping CSRF tokens because 'our API only accepts JSON'
Setting long-lived access tokens without a refresh mechanism
Not validating the token audience or issuer on the backend

data.title: Audit token storage
data.description: Find every place in your project where tokens or secrets are stored or transmitted. Classify each by risk level and propose a safer alternative.
steps: Search for localStorage, sessionStorage, document.cookie, and window.name
Search for tokens in Redux, Zustand, or other global stores
Check fetch and axios calls for Authorization headers using client-side tokens
Review the server's Set-Cookie headers for Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite
Document findings and write a remediation plan
data.expectedOutcome: You should have a clear map of every token touchpoint, the associated risk, and a prioritized list of fixes.

items.question: What if we need the token for a third-party API?
items.answer: Create a backend proxy endpoint that exchanges the HttpOnly session for a short-lived API key, or use OAuth 2.0 with PKCE so the access token never touches your page storage.

items.question: Are HttpOnly cookies vulnerable to CSRF?
items.answer: Yes, because the browser sends them automatically with cross-site requests. Mitigate with SameSite=Lax, SameSite=Strict, or a double-submit CSRF cookie pattern for write operations.

items.question: What about passwordless magic links?
items.answer: Magic links are tokens too. Store the session in an HttpOnly cookie after the magic link callback, and do not store the link token in localStorage.

items.question: How do I debug auth issues without the token in localStorage?
items.answer: Use the Network tab to inspect Set-Cookie and Cookie headers. Use server logs to verify token issuance. Avoid console.log of sensitive values in production.

data.title: Summary
points: Never store access tokens in localStorage or sessionStorage
Prefer HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies managed by the server
Implement refresh token rotation and short-lived access tokens
Mitigate CSRF with SameSite cookies or double-submit tokens
Treat every token touchpoint as a potential security incident
data.takeaway: A senior engineer reviews authentication not as a checkbox, but as an ongoing negotiation between usability and attack surface.
